papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Early detection of exacerbations of asthma or COPD increases the chances of positive treatment outcomes. In the TACTICAS (Telemonitoring for Asthma and COPD Through voICe AnalysiS) study, a prospective cohort study, we investigated if voice changes during an exacerbation and which voice features signify the onset of an exacerbation. METHODS: In a cohort of 73 participants (35 asthma, 38 COPD) with a mean age of 62 years, daily voice was collected at home on their own mobile devices for 3 months. Simultaneously, the time course (onset, peak and recovery) of an exacerbation was captured using the Exacerbations of Chronic Pulmonary Disease Tool (EXACT) questionnaire. We performed a random intercept multilevel analysis to investigate changes in 39 speech features during onset (first day of exacerbation), peak (day of highest symptoms burden) and recovery (symptom relief). A total of 38 exacerbations from 35 participants were captured within the study period, most of which were mild and moderate in severity. RESULTS: Voice changes already occurred at exacerbation onset, where 13 features had a significant fixed effect. Specifically, features such as the duration of sustained vowels decreased, while shimmer (irregularity of vocal fold vibrations) and noise-to-harmonics ratio increased, indicating the deterioration of overall voice quality during an exacerbation. CONCLUSIONS: We found that voice significantly changes during an exacerbation of asthma or COPD, and this occurs as early as at exacerbation onset. These findings highlight the potential of voice as biomarker for early detection and management of exacerbations. It also addresses the unmet need of remote patient monitoring via mobile devices in the home environment using novel digital biomarkers.

papers.abstract_en: RATIONALE: Inhaled aztreonam improves symptoms in bronchiectasis, with baseline bacterial load predicting therapeutic responses in Western populations. Evidence for inhaled tobramycin, a widely used alternative, remained limited in non-Western countries. The objectives of the present study were to investigate how baseline bacterial load modulates symptomatic responses to inhaled tobramycin, and to identify which symptoms improved most favourably in bronchiectasis. METHODS: A post hoc analysis of the TORNASOL randomised, placebo-controlled trial included 357 adults with bronchiectasis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in China. Patients received inhaled tobramycin or placebo in two 28-day on-off cycles, with follow-up to day 85. Sputum bacterial load was stratified as high (≥107 CFU·g-1), moderate (105-106 CFU·g-1) and low (<105 CFU·g-1) load. Changes in the total Quality-of-Life Bronchiectasis Respiratory Symptom Scores (QoL-B-RSS; minimal clinically important difference (MCID): 8 points) and individual symptom domains were analysed, with Bonferroni correction applied to the nine-item-level comparisons (adjusted α=0.0056). RESULTS: At baseline, 68.3% of patients had high and 29.1% had moderate bacterial load, with >75% of high-load patients remaining in the same category. Compared with placebo, inhaled tobramycin yielded significant QoL-B-RSS improvements exceeding MCID in the high-load subgroup (mean difference 8.28, 95% CI 4.46-12.09; p<0.0001) and below the MCID in the moderate-load subgroup (mean difference 6.51, 95% CI 1.31-11.72; p=0.0065) at day 29, with improvements at day 85. Cough, sputum production/purulence and chest congestion were the symptoms exhibiting most favourable responses, particularly in the high-load subgroup. CONCLUSIONS: High bacterial load was associated with numerically greater symptomatic improvements to inhaled tobramycin in bronchiectasis. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant further investigation.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Delayed intubation in lung cancer patients receiving high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy is associated with increased mortality. Reliable bedside tools are essential for early risk stratification. We aimed to compare the predictive performance of the ROX index and HACOR score for the early identification of HFNC failure in this high-risk population. METHODS: This retrospective observational study included 176 ICU patients with lung cancer and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure who received HFNC. Time-point analyses of the ROX index and HACOR score at 1 and 3 h were restricted to patients with complete physiological data at both time points (n = 88). The primary outcome was clinician-determined HFNC failure, defined as endotracheal intubation within 48 h after HFNC initiation. RESULTS: HFNC failure occurred in 50 of 176 patients (28.4%) in the overall cohort and in 39 of 88 patients (44.3%) in the complete-case analytical cohort. Patients who required endotracheal intubation exhibited higher baseline illness severity (SOFA and APACHE II) and persistent tachypnea. At the 3-hour assessment, the ROX index showed higher observed discrimination than the HACOR score (AUROC 0.860 [95% CI 0.760-0.960] vs. 0.740 [95% CI 0.590-0.890]). Only the prespecified 1- and 3-hour time points were evaluated; therefore, these findings do not establish 3 h as the optimal assessment time. In an exploratory analysis in which the threshold was derived and evaluated in the same analytical cohort, a 3-hour ROX value ≤ 5.1 identified patients at higher risk of HFNC failure; this threshold has not been independently validated. Respiratory rate alone also showed high prognostic value at 3 h (AUROC 0.850 [95% CI 0.730-0.970]). CONCLUSION: Within the complete-case cohort, which represented half of the overall population, the 3-hour ROX index showed higher observed discrimination for clinician-determined HFNC failure than HACOR. However, selection and incorporation bias may have affected this comparison. The data-derived threshold should not be used as a stand-alone intubation criterion and requires prospective validation using standardized serial measurements and independently adjudicated outcomes. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable; this was a retrospective observational study.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Airway secretion retention represents a major clinical challenge in critically ill patients, promoting gas exchange impairment and atelectasis, precipitating failure of noninvasive respiratory support, and prolonging invasive mechanical ventilation, with an associated increase in respiratory-related complications and mortality. High-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO) is a noninvasive airway clearance technique widely used in chronic respiratory diseases, but its role in the intensive care unit (ICU) remains unclear. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the available evidence on the efficacy and safety of HFCWO in adult ICU patients. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Library from inception to December 2025 in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Studies evaluating HFCWO in adult ICU patients, including those receiving invasive or noninvasive respiratory support, were eligible. Primary outcomes included duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, and mortality. Secondary outcomes included impact on secretion airway clearance and its radiographic/functional surrogates as well as safety and treatment tolerance. RESULTS: A limited number of studies met the inclusion criteria, mainly small randomized controlled trials and observational studies, characterized by substantial heterogeneity in patient populations, intervention protocols, and assessed outcomes. HFCWO effects on clinically meaningful primary endpoints, including duration of mechanical ventilation, length of ICU stay, and mortality, remain variable and inconclusive. Overall, HFCWO was well tolerated and appeared to enhance secretion clearance, with some studies reporting modest improvements in oxygenation and respiratory mechanics. CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence suggests that HFCWO is a safe and feasible airway clearance strategy in selected ICU patients with secretion burden and without proved effects on the main clinical outcomes. Lack of physiopathologically driven criteria for selection of patients more likely to respond to HFCWO either alone or integrated with other cough-assisting techniques may partially explain these scanty findings from the overall published studies. This precludes its routine use in clinical practice. Well-designed, adequately powered randomized trials are needed to define patient selection criteria, optimal timing, and the true clinical impact of HFCWO in the ICU setting.

papers.abstract_en: In the era of precision targeted therapy, anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have significantly improved survival outcomes for patients with ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The third-generation ALK inhibitor lorlatinib, characterized by superior antitumor activity, a broader spectrum of ALK mutation sites and enhanced central nervous system (CNS) penetrability, has yielded breakthrough clinical benefits. However, lorlatinib has a distinct adverse event profile, with edema, dyslipidemia, central and peripheral nervous system toxicities, posing key clinical management challenges. Herein, we report the first case of an ALK-fusion NSCLC patient who developed peripheral neuropathy, dysarthria, and sensorineural deafness following lorlatinib treatment. While dysarthria and peripheral neuropathy have been previously documented, sensorineural deafness is extremely rare, and no prior reports describe the concurrent and persistent onset of all three symptoms, underscoring the need for enhanced toxicity monitoring and patient education.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Breathlessness intervention services (BIS) coach people with chronic illness to self-manage persistent breathlessness using non-pharmacological strategies like positioning, breathing techniques and airflow. The Australian Capital Territory BIS (ABIS) Project aimed to co-design, implement and evaluate the feasibility of a home-based BIS delivered by a private physiotherapy provider. ABIS was evaluated against two goals: 1) 100 patients completing the program within 12 months; 2) ≥ 75% of patients reporting benefit on ≥ 1 outcome. METHODS: ABIS and its evaluation framework were co-designed by persons with breathlessness, carers, clinicians and researchers. Patients were referred by GPs/medical specialists. Number of visits was tailored to patient/carer need. Evaluation used a mixed methods approach. Quantitative data consisted of process measures and clinical assessments double-purposed as outcome measures. Qualitative data included team meeting minutes and semi-structured interviews with patients, carers and referrers. The project team convened after 3-monthly plan-do-study-act (PDSA) cycles to review data and decide service refinements. Findings were integrated using the RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) Framework. RESULTS: Reach: In the first 12 months, 64 patients completed the program, falling short of the 100 goal. Over 22 months, 140 patients completed ABIS (4% of the eligible population), including people who were older, less mobile and unable to access rehabilitation. EFFECTIVENESS: All patients reported improvements on ≥ 1 outcome: 90% on activities of daily living (ADLs), 70% 'worst' breathlessness, and 68% mastery. 21% reported having avoided calling an ambulance for breathlessness using the strategies they had learned through ABIS. As participants' ADLs increased, breathlessness severity and mastery tended to worsen temporarily, with number of follow-ups being largely determined by how quickly mastery could be regained. 79% of carers reported improved confidence in supporting breathlessness. Adoption: GP engagement remained limited, with 47% referrals from specialist care. IMPLEMENTATION: The median number of visits was 4 (range 1-6). Mean cost per-patient was AUD1,576.86. Maintenance: Most patients maintained outcomes at 3/6-month follow-up. ABIS built system-level capacity for provision of ongoing breathlessness support after the project period. CONCLUSIONS: The ABIS Project offers new insights to inform community BIS design and adaptation. Future trials should compare cost-effectiveness of single- versus multi-disciplinary BIS.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is the most frequent nosocomial infection in critically ill patients. Local pH variations affect bacterial growth. This study investigated the role and mechanisms of airspace acidification by mechanical ventilation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa-induced VAP to test the hypothesis that overventilation-induced airspace acidification promotes Pseudomonas aeruginosa adhesion and increases susceptibility to pneumonia. METHODS: Mice were subjected to high tidal volume (HVt: 34 mL·kg-1) or low tidal volume (LVt: 9 mL·kg-1) mechanical ventilation and intratracheally infected with P. aeruginosa. Relative airspace acidification was estimated via fluorescence microscopy in murine lungs ex vivo. Bacterial growth and adhesion on cyclically stretched A549 and human alveolar epithelial cells was examined. RESULTS: Upon P. aeruginosa infection, HVt mice showed significantly increased alveolo-capillary permeability, elevated lung and blood leukocyte counts, and higher bacterial load in lungs and extrapulmonary organs as compared to LVt controls. HVt mechanical ventilation increased airspace acidification signal in lungs ex vivo and significantly decreased pulmonary expression of Na+/H+exchanger (NHE)1. Inhibition of NHE1 significantly enhanced P. aeruginosa growth on alveolar epithelial cells in vitro and increased pulmonary bacterial loads in LVt-mechanical ventilation mice in vivo. CONCLUSION: In a novel murine VAP model, key characteristics of P. aeruginosa-VAP were replicated. HVt mechanical ventilation induced mild ventilator-induced lung injury with acidification of airspace lining fluid, increasing susceptibility to P. aeruginosa pneumonia. NHE1-dependent pH regulation was identified as a mechanistic contributor to ventilation-associated airspace acidification and subsequent pulmonary infection susceptibility, representing a candidate target for therapeutic modulation in P. aeruginosa-VAP.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Genetic factors play an important role in the pathogenesis of interstitial lung diseases. Recent studies have shown that approximately 30% of familial interstitial lung diseases are associated with mutations in telomere-related genes. Herein, we present a young patient with severe pulmonary fibrosis and multisystem involvement in whom a homozygous NOP10 variant was identified. CASE REPORT: A 29-year-old man presented with progressive exertional dyspnea, cough, and fever. Thoracic computed tomography demonstrated a probable usual interstitial pneumonia pattern. Laboratory investigations showed anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase levels, while hematological evaluation revealed a hypocellular bone marrow. Abdominal imaging demonstrated findings compatible with chronic liver disease. Due to parental consanguinity and a positive family history, alpha-1 antitrypsin analysis and whole-exome sequencing (WES) were performed. Despite treatment, his clinical condition continued to deteriorate, with progression to multiorgan failure, and he died on the 21st day of hospitalization. Genetic results obtained after the patient's death revealed the presence of the alpha-1 antitrypsin Pi*M/P Lowell variant and the homozygous NOP10 variant. CONCLUSION: In conclusion, to the best of our knowledge, this case is the first to describe a patient with a homozygous NOP10 p.Arg34Trp variant who presented with severe pulmonary fibrosis and multisystem involvement in the absence of the classic mucocutaneous triad of dyskeratosis congenita (nail dystrophy, reticular skin pigmentation, and oral leukoplakia).

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Breathlessness has long been associated with respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. Obesity has also been reported to be independently associated with breathlessness. However, the impact of obesity on lung volumes and diffusion capacity parameters among those with breathlessness who showed no evidence of respiratory or cardiac disease has not been well explored, particularly in Saudi Arabia. Thus, the aims of this study were (1) to assess whether body mass index (BMI) is associated with lung volumes and diffusion capacity parameters, and (2) to explore the impact of overweight and obesity on lung volumes and diffusion capacity parameters among Saudi participants who visited a pulmonary clinic for a follow-up concerning unexplained breathlessness. METHOD: The medical records of individuals who visited our local respiratory clinic complaining of breathlessness and underwent a full pulmonary function test were reviewed. Participants with known respiratory or cardiovascular diseases and missing lung volumes and diffusion capacity data were excluded. Group comparisons across BMI categories (normal weight, overweight, and obesity) were performed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's multiple comparisons test. Associations between BMI and lung function parameters were further evaluated using multivariable linear regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, and smoking status. RESULTS: A total of 79 patients met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final analyses, of whom 62% were male. The means ± SD age and BMI were 47 ± 15.5 years and 29.7 ± 7.2 kg/m2, respectively. Expiratory reserve volume (ERV), functional residual capacity (FRC), and DLCO (% predicted) were lower in obese participants compared with normal weight and/or overweight groups. In multivariable analysis, BMI remained independently associated with reduced ERV (β = -1.83, 95% CI - 2.74 to - 0.91, p < 0.0001) and DLCO (β = -0.69, 95% CI - 1.15 to - 0.23, p < 0.001), and a modest increase in inspiratory capacity (IC) (β = 0.62, 95% CI 0.05 to 1.20, p < 0.05), with no significant associations observed for other lung volumes. CONCLUSION: Obesity was associated with lower ERV and DLCO in individuals with unexplained breathlessness. These findings support pulmonary function assessment and weight management in clinical practice. Further studies are needed to explore the underlying mechanisms of obesity and its associations with breathlessness and impairment in lung function.

papers.abstract_en: PURPOSE: MDA5+ dermatomyositis (MDA5+DM) frequently complicates interstitial lung disease (ILD), especially rapidly progressive ILD (RP-ILD), which worsens prognosis. Traditional assessments cannot directly reflect fibroblast activation status, a key driver of pulmonary fibrosis. 68Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT targets fibroblast activation protein (FAP), but its value in MDA5+DM remains understudied. METHODS: Fourteen MDA5+DM patients and 5 controls were enrolled. 68Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT was performed to obtain SUVmax of lungs, muscles, and other organs. Clinical data, pulmonary function tests, and deep learning-quantified HRCT indices were collected. Follow-ups for pulmonary function and HRCT were conducted. Correlations between SUVmax, clinical features, and follow-up outcomes were analyzed. RESULTS: Whole-lung SUVmax was significantly higher in MDA5+DM patients (3.32 vs. 0.67, p < 0.0001), with left lower lobe showing the most prominent difference (p = 0.0003). SUVmax strongly correlated with HRCT inflammation/fibrosis indices (e.g., left lower lobe vs. PII at 3 months: r = 0.9863, p < 0.0001) and small-to-medium airway function (lung vs. MMEF 75/25: r=-0.8168, p = 0.0133). Baseline SUVmax predicted 3-12-month lesion progression and lung function changes, with deceased patients having higher baseline whole-lung SUVmax (p = 0.008). CONCLUSION: This exploratory study suggests that 68Ga-FAPI-04 PET/CT may reflect fibroblast activation and the active inflammatory-fibrotic process, assesses early pulmonary impairments and monitoring lesion progression in MDA5+DM. It provides a valuable hypothesis-generating tool for clinical evaluation, warranting further validation.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Despite advances in asthma management, asthma exacerbations (AE) remain a leading cause of morbidity, and the immunopathological mechanisms driving AE progression need further clarification. Here, we explored the role of macrophage apoptosis resistance in AE using clinical samples and murine models. METHODS: Macrophages were isolated from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) of AE patients and lung macrophages from AE mice to detect Bcl-2 expression and apoptosis. We performed adoptive transfer of ex vivo apoptotic bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) and ADAM8-silenced BMDMs. Integrative transcriptomic analysis of GSE144576 combined with in vivo validation was used to screen regulators of lung macrophage apoptosis resistance. In vitro and in vivo experiments with the peptidomimetic inhibitor BK1361 were conducted to dissect ADAM8 downstream signaling. RESULTS: Macrophages from AE patients and AE mice showed elevated Bcl-2 and strong apoptosis resistance. Adoptive transfer of apoptotic BMDMs partially reversed macrophage apoptosis resistance and mitigated airway inflammation. Transcriptomics plus animal validation identified ADAM8 as a regulator of macrophage apoptosis resistance. Consistently, transfer of ADAM8-silenced BMDMs relieved airway inflammation and reduced apoptosis resistance. Mechanistically, ADAM8 may activate PI3K/AKT signaling to upregulate Bcl-2 and promote apoptosis resistance. BK1361 suppressed ADAM8/PI3K/AKT signaling, enhanced macrophage apoptosis, and reduced inflammatory infiltration, mucus hypersecretion, and airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) in AE mice. DISCUSSION: In summary, macrophage apoptosis resistance drives inflammatory amplification in AE. The ADAM8/PI3K/AKT axis mediates this phenotype, indicating ADAM8 as a promising therapeutic target for AE.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Chronic helminth infection is associated with altered anti-mycobacterial immunity, including impaired Th1 responses and expansion of regulatory immune populations. However, how helminth infection reshapes coordinated innate and adaptive immune pathways during active tuberculosis remains poorly understood. We therefore investigated systemic and cellular immune signatures associated with helminth infection, tuberculosis (TB), and helminth-TB coinfection. METHODS: Plasma and peripheral blood mononuclear cells were obtained from healthy Swedish controls, endemic Peruvian controls, individuals with helminth infection, active tuberculosis, and helminth-TB coinfection. Plasma proteins were quantified using high-throughput Olink proteomics, while circulating monocytes and CD4+ T-cell compartments were characterized via flow cytometry. Protein abundance, monocyte phenotypes, and CD4+ T-cell differentiation and activation marker expression were compared between study groups. RESULTS: Proteomic profiling revealed broad differences associated with active TB, whereas helminth infection alone was associated with relatively few differentially abundant proteins compared with endemic controls. Participants with helminth-TB coinfection exhibited 65 differentially abundant proteins compared with endemic controls, including 33 that met the significance threshold only in this comparison. These proteins were associated with immune regulation, leukocyte trafficking, vascular activation, and myeloid responses. Flow cytometric analysis revealed increased PD-L1 expression on intermediate monocytes in helminth-infected participants compared to endemic controls, while plasma CD274 abundance was highest in helminth-TB coinfection. Coinfected individuals also displayed increased IL-4 receptor expression on classical and intermediate monocytes compared to the endemic control group. Within the CD4+ T-cell compartment, helminth infection was associated with broad upregulation of PD-1 across naïve, central memory, effector memory, and effector subsets, whereas TB was associated with altered T-cell differentiation and increased TIM-3 expression. Helminth-TB coinfection combined these features and was further characterized by increased frequencies of CTLA-4+, CD40L+, and CD28+ CD4+ T-cell populations. CONCLUSION: Plasma proteomic and cellular profiling identified distinct immune signatures associated with TB, helminth infection, and their co-occurrence. Helminth-TB coinfection was associated with additional changes in immune regulation and cell-communication pathways, alongside concurrent activation-associated and inhibitory features across monocyte and CD4+ T-cell compartments. Together, these findings support an exploratory model in which active TB is associated with broad systemic inflammatory remodeling, while helminth exposure is associated with an additional regulatory overlay during coinfection.

papers.abstract_en: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a complex and heterogeneous disease affecting approximately 300 million individuals worldwide. Currently, there is an unmet need in the management of COPD, leading to some patients receiving inadequate or inappropriate treatment. The aim of this paper is to synthesize expert opinion from a group of Europe-based pulmonologists from nine countries on the unmet needs and challenges in the patient pathway for COPD and to outline potential recommendations to address them. In order to explore the current gaps and potential solutions in clinical practice, patients diagnosed with COPD with unmet needs were divided into two groups: 1) patients not receiving optimal treatment and 2) patients with access to standard treatment options, but with unmet needs due to continuing symptom burden or exacerbations. Key challenges for patients suboptimally treated center around inadequate treatment intensification and device mismatch/inhaler technique, with proposed solutions focusing on disease stability and considerations around patient dexterity and cognitive status for inhaler choice and technique. For patients with unmet needs despite optimized inhaled treatment, challenges focus on recurrent exacerbations, with proposed solutions of personalized treatment assessing phenotypes and endotypes which may inform timely initiation of additional treatments, such as biologics. Hereby, we discuss the multifactorial issues that contribute to unmet needs, and how a shift in the paradigm of COPD management is necessary to tackle the gap in patient care.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Invasive mold disease (IMD) remains a substantial cause of patient morbidity and mortality. Aspergillosis and mucormycosis remain the predominant infections encountered, although rare molds continue to emerge as important pathogens. Improvement in patient outcomes has been the result of progress in risk stratification, diagnostics, supportive care, antifungal therapy, and/or prophylaxis, yet substantial challenges remain, requiring the development of novel treatment strategies. Clinical trials evaluating treatment response are currently based on consensus criteria published in 2008. However, advances in clinical mycology and the broadening variety of mold diseases in clinical trials necessitate a revision of these criteria to ensure that adjudication of patient outcomes accurately captures responses to therapeutic intervention. METHODS: To tackle this task, an international expert panel nominated by the European Confederation of Medical Mycology (ECMM) and Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium (MSGERC) was convened. RESULTS: The panel produced updated consensus guidance for assessing treatment responses and defining study outcomes in clinical trials of IMD in both adults and children. CONCLUSIONS: Along with guidance, potential pitfalls in assessing outcome, such as discordant clinical, radiologic, and/or mycologic data and areas for future research are discussed.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a leading cause of disease- related mortality worldwide and is characterized by progressive airflow limitation accompanied by persistent neutrophilic airway inflammation. Macrophage activation plays a key role in this process through the production of pro- inflammatory mediators and neutrophil-attracting chemokines. METHODS: This study investigated the anti-inflammatory effects of Cardamine flexuosa extract (CFE) in macrophage and cigarette smoke extract (CSE)/lipopolysaccharide (LPS)- induced models, with emphasis on macrophage inflammatory responses and neutrophilic airway inflammation. RESULTS: In LPS-stimulated RAW 264.7 macrophages, CFE reduced nitric oxide production by 77.8% and decreased the secretion of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), accompanied by reduced MAPK phosphorylation. In a murine model induced by intranasal administration of CSE and LPS, oral CFE reduced total inflammatory cell and neutrophil counts in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) by 53.9% and 82.9%, respectively, at 200 mg/kg compared with the CSE/LPS group. These effects were associated with reduced pulmonary expression of CXCL-1 and MIP-2 and decreased MAPK phosphorylation. Histological analysis demonstrated attenuation of inflammatory cell infiltration and mucus hypersecretion. CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate that CFE attenuates macrophage inflammatory responses and neutrophilic airway inflammation in the CSE/LPS-induced murine model, accompanied by reduced inflammatory mediator production and MAPK activation.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Pulmonary rehabilitation (PR) is beneficial, yet outcome assessment remains inconsistent. A multidisciplinary D-A-CH working group reviewed evidence, introduced new measures, and explored emerging PR concepts. SUMMARY: The meeting emphasized patient-reported and clinician-reported outcome measures. A key focus was the minimal clinically important difference (MCID), a widely used metric which is applied inconsistently and is highly dependent on the baseline value. The "performance score" (T2D = T2 + (T2-T1)) takes baseline status (T1) into account by combining the discharge value (T2) with the improvement (T2-T1) before and after treatment, based on the distribution. This simple descriptive approach results in a baseline-adjusted MCID estimator, with a planned multicenter study to validate its use in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease rehabilitation. Further discussions addressed epistemic trust, crucial for patient adherence and interdisciplinary collaboration, with a study planned to assess its impact. Dysfunctional breathing (DB), often overlooked in PR, was highlighted, emphasizing the need for standardized diagnostic tools. The role of artificial intelligence (AI) in PR, including large language models, was explored, with surveys planned to evaluate patient and provider perceptions. KEY MESSAGES: The T2D performance score offers a dynamic approach to assessing PR progress, addressing MCID limitations. Standardized methods for epistemic trust and DB diagnosis are essential for better recognition and management. AI integration in PR presents opportunities for personalized rehabilitation but requires further evaluation. The D-A-CH working group remains committed to advancing PR through evidence-based strategies and international collaboration.

papers.abstract_en: This paper outlines the critical role of General Practitioners (GPs) in managing allergic rhinitis (AR) and asthma, two prevalent chronic respiratory diseases characterized by immune-mediated airway inflammation. AR and asthma frequently coexist, affecting an increasing portion of the global population and imposing substantial health and socioeconomic burdens. The paper highlights that GPs are often the first point of contact for patients and are uniquely positioned to ensure early diagnosis, ongoing care, and adherence to evidence-based treatment guidelines. It emphasizes the necessity of integrated, multidisciplinary approaches, including collaboration with specialists and pharmacists, to enhance patient outcomes and optimize healthcare resources. Challenges such as fragmented care, regional disparities in healthcare access, and patient self-medication are discussed, underscoring the need for structured healthcare pathways and the more effective use of diagnostic tools. The article also emphasizes the growing importance of digital health technologies, telemedicine, and artificial intelligence in supporting GPs, improving adherence monitoring, and personalizing patient management. Ultimately, empowering GPs through education, resource allocation, and stronger multidisciplinary networks is essential to improve the management of AR and asthma, mitigating their impact on patients' quality of life, and ensuring better sustainability of care.
